Tracker Case Study
TrackerUX/UI case study
Self-initiated concept · Desktop and phone widget

One small widget for the notes, plans and progress that usually live in five places.

Tracker brings sticky notes, a daily plan, weekly habits and a calendar into one window, and shows you how much you have actually finished. This case study covers who I designed for, what went wrong in my first version, and why the second one looks the way it does.

Project
Tracker, a productivity widget
Tagline
Plan. Track. Grow.
My focus
Research, UX decisions, UI, iteration
Views designed
Notes, Day, Week, Calendar
Overview

People forget small tasks, and nothing shows them how far they have come.

The problem

Tasks end up on sticky notes, in calendars and across several apps. When people finally sit down to work, they are trying to remember everything at once.

The goal

A simple, visual way to stay consistent with daily goals. Tracker keeps tasks organized so people can focus on getting them done.

The result

A four-view widget where every view answers one question: what do I need to remember, do today, do this week, and how consistent have I been?

Users

Who I designed for

The idea applies to anyone juggling more than one list. I grouped the audience into five, then wrote two personas to test my decisions against.

  • Students and learners
  • Working professionals
  • Job seekers and career switchers
  • Self-improvement enthusiasts
  • Freelancers and creators

Riya Sharma, the busy professional

28 · Marketing executive

Works full time and tries to fit in fitness, learning and personal interests. She struggles to keep a consistent routine across all of them.

Goals

  • Organize daily activities
  • Balance work and personal life
  • Track weekly productivity

Pain points

  • Frequently misses planned tasks
  • Struggles with time management

Arjun Mehta, the aspiring learner

24 · Student and job seeker

Focused on learning new skills and building a career. He makes daily schedules, then loses track of his progress and his motivation.

Goals

  • Learn new skills
  • Build his career
  • Stay motivated

Pain points

  • Gets distracted easily
  • Struggles to follow schedules
  • Finds it hard to measure progress
Research

Existing tools are good, but none of them are small and visual.

I reviewed four popular apps to see where a lightweight widget could fit. I was not looking for weaknesses. I was looking for the job nobody was doing.

AppGap I noticed
TodoistExtensive task features that can feel heavy for someone who wants a quick daily overview.
Microsoft To DoYou open the app and move between lists to review different kinds of tasks.
Google TasksFocused on lists and scheduling, with no mix of sticky notes and progress tracking.
Notion CalendarBuilt around events and scheduling, not quick capture and completion tracking.

The openingQuick capture and visible progress, in one place, without the weight of a full task manager. That became the brief for Tracker.

Decisions

Five problems, five decisions, and the reason behind each

Problem

Scattered tasks

People switch between sticky notes, calendars and several apps, so nothing feels organized.

Decision

One workspace for notes and tasks

Why: Every extra app is another place to check. Putting notes next to the plan removes the switching, which is where tasks get dropped.

Problem

Forgotten reminders

On busy days, small but important tasks slip away when memory is the only system.

Decision

A quick-access sticky note view

Why: A reminder has to be captured in seconds or it does not get captured. Sticky notes are a format people already trust for this, and they stay in view.

Problem

Unstructured planning

Users find it hard to organize tasks across daily, weekly and monthly schedules.

Decision

Day, Week and Calendar views

Why: People plan at three zoom levels: today, this week, this month. Giving each its own view means nobody has to squeeze all three into one list.

Problem

No progress visibility

Without an overview, it is hard to see what is finished or how productive you have been.

Decision

Completion indicators and percentages

Why: Both personas lose motivation when they cannot see effort add up. A number and a bar turn a finished task into evidence of progress.

Problem

Overwhelming interfaces

Many tools offer so many features that simple task management feels complicated.

Decision

Essential features and clean navigation

Why: My research showed that power often arrives as complexity. Four tabs, one job each, keeps the widget something you can read in a glance.

Iteration

First version, second version

My first screens were clean and functional. Comparing them side by side showed me what they could not do. The second round changed behaviour, not just looks.

Notes

Quick search and stronger hierarchy

The first version was a text box and a list with a delete icon. That works for two notes and fails at twenty. I added search and an add button above the notes, and turned each note into a yellow card with its date.

Why: Once notes pile up, finding one becomes the main job. The yellow cards also separate content from controls at a glance.

Day

Hourly scheduling

The first Day view was a checklist of five items. It said what to do and nothing about when. The new version is an hourly timeline with a marker for the current time.

Why: A checklist lets everything stay vague. Hourly slots make you place work in time, which supports better time management, the exact struggle Riya has.

Week

Progress tracking and a tabular layout

Before, each weekday had one checkbox. After, a progress card sits above a table where each habit, such as Lunch or Meditation, has its own column.

Why: One checkbox per day cannot tell you what you did. A table makes status easy to compare across days and habits, and the percentage answers “how am I doing?” before you read a single row.

Calendar

Progress over time

The first calendar only highlighted today. The new one shows monthly progress at the top and a small completion ring inside each day.

Why: Tracking and productivity are different things. A record of what you finished matters less than seeing how consistent you have been over weeks, so the calendar became a history of effort.

A colour system with one job per colour

TealActive tab, progress bars and completed states.
YellowUsed only for sticky notes, so notes are always easy to spot.
OrangeOne thin line for the current time in the Day view.
Dark surfaceA quiet base, so the three accents carry the meaning.
Learnings

What went wrong and what I took from it

My assumptions were not always right

I started with the belief that a simple checklist was enough. It was not. A checkbox records that something is done, but users also need to see how their time and effort turn into progress.

What I changed: progress bars, percentages and daily rings.

More information does not mean more clarity

Adding features without thinking about how they relate made the interface harder to read. Organizing what was already there mattered more than adding more.

What I changed: grouped content into clear sections, with a progress summary above the detail.

Tracking and productivity are different

Recording completed tasks does not make someone productive. Showing progress over time gives a better picture of consistency.

What I changed: weekly and monthly progress, so the widget reports on habits and not only on single tasks.

Small design decisions can change behaviour

Hourly slots and the table layout made me think beyond task management, toward how the interface itself can encourage better time management.

What I changed: the Day view now asks “when?”, and the Week view asks “which habit?”.

The first design is rarely the final answer

Putting my first and second screens next to each other exposed problems I had not noticed. Iterating taught me to question my decisions instead of defending them.

What I changed: I now compare versions side by side before I call a screen done.

Next

What I would do next

Test with real people

My second round came from my own critique. I want to watch people like Riya and Arjun use it and see whether hourly slots really change how they plan.

Check small text

Table headers and calendar labels in the dark theme are small. I would test contrast and text size against accessibility guidelines and raise them where needed.

Design the phone version

The concept mockup shows Tracker on a phone. The next step is a layout made for touch, with larger targets and quick note capture.
